Predicting Olist delivery_days with linear, regularized, and decision tree models

Overview and Target / Leakage Guardrails

This analysis builds models that predict delivery_days (days from order purchase to customer delivery) using only information that is available when an order is placed or approved. It starts from the cleaned order-item dataset prepared on the Data page, engineers route, product, and timing features, and compares three feature recipes across four model families, plus benchmarks, on a held-out test set.

Design choices

  • Split by order, not by row. The data has one row per order item, and delivery_days repeats across the items of an order. If items from one order landed in both training and test data, the test score would be inflated. Every split below keeps all items of an order together.
  • Train / validation / test, no cross-validation. Model settings are chosen on a validation set carved out of the training data. The test set is used once, at the end.
  • Three recipes that add one group of features at a time, so we can see what each group contributes.
  • Four model families: linear regression, ridge, lasso, and a decision tree.
  • Metrics in days. We keep delivery_days on its raw scale so errors are directly interpretable. MAE (average absolute error) is the primary metric, RMSE (which penalizes large misses more) is secondary, and R² is the traditional version, 1 - SSE/SST on the test set. An R² of 0 means no better than predicting the average; it can be negative.

What was kept out of the predictors, and why

Step 1: Checking skewness of delivery_days

Before splitting, we compare the mean, median, and the log10(delivery_days) histogram to see whether the target is right-skewed. The log10 histogram excludes zero-day rows because \(\log_{10}(0)\) is undefined.

Code 
df_clean <- read_rds("data/df_master_clean.rds")

skew_check_tbl <- df_clean |>
  summarise(
    min_days = min(delivery_days),
    n_zero_days = sum(delivery_days == 0),
    mean_days = mean(delivery_days),
    median_days = median(delivery_days),
    max_days = max(delivery_days),
    sd_days = sd(delivery_days),
    n_rows = n()
  )

kable(
  skew_check_tbl,
  digits = 2,
  format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
  col.names = c("Min", "Zero-Day Rows", "Mean", "Median", "Max", "SD", "Rows"),
  caption = "Skewness check on delivery_days before splitting"
)
Skewness check on delivery_days before splitting
Min Zero-Day Rows Mean Median Max SD Rows

Code 
ggplot(df_clean |> filter(delivery_days > 0), aes(x = log10(delivery_days))) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "#1b9e77", color = "white", alpha = 0.9) +
  labs(
    title = "log10(delivery_days) pulls in the right tail",
    subtitle = "Zero-day rows excluded from this chart only",
    x = "log10(delivery_days)",
    y = "Order-item count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

Across the 110,196 cleaned order-item rows, delivery_days is right-skewed: the mean (12.01 days) exceeds the median (10 days), the standard deviation is 9.45 days, and the tail reaches 209 days. A log transform would make the distribution more symmetric, but we keep the raw scale so that MAE and RMSE stay directly interpretable in days for a logistics manager.

Step 2: Feature engineering

We build features in four groups: route (where the item travels), timing, product and order characteristics, and Olist’s own checkout estimate.

Code 
df_model <- df_clean |>
  # Order size: how many items, and how many different sellers, share one order
  group_by(order_id) |>
  mutate(n_items = n(), n_sellers = n_distinct(seller_id)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(
    # Handling time the seller was given before the item had to ship
    ship_window_days = as.numeric(difftime(shipping_limit_date,
                                           order_purchase_timestamp, units = "days")),
    # Package size, density, and shipping cost relative to item value
    volume_cm3    = product_length_cm * product_height_cm * product_width_cm,
    density_g_cm3 = product_weight_g / pmax(volume_cm3, 1),
    freight_ratio = freight_value / price,
    # Route features. Coordinates are not available, so distance is approximated by a
    # same-state flag and by the first digit of the zip prefix (a coarse geographic region)
    same_state    = factor(if_else(seller_state == customer_state, "same", "different")),
    cust_region   = factor(substr(sprintf("%05d", as.integer(customer_zip_code_prefix)), 1, 1)),
    seller_region = factor(substr(sprintf("%05d", as.integer(seller_zip_code_prefix)), 1, 1)),
    same_region   = factor(if_else(cust_region == seller_region, "same", "different")),
    # Timing and category fields are treated as categories, because seasonality
    # (for example a slow month) is not a straight-line effect
    purchase_year  = factor(purchase_year),
    purchase_month = factor(purchase_month),
    purchase_dow   = factor(purchase_day_of_week),
    customer_state = factor(customer_state),
    seller_state   = factor(seller_state),
    category       = factor(product_category_name_english)
  ) |>
  select(order_id, delivery_days, estimated_days,
         customer_state, seller_state, same_state, cust_region, seller_region,
         same_region, purchase_year, purchase_month, purchase_dow,
         freight_value, price, freight_ratio, product_weight_g, volume_cm3,
         density_g_cm3, n_items, n_sellers, ship_window_days, category,
         product_photos_qty, product_name_length, product_description_length)

Step 3: Train / validation / test split, grouped by order

We hold out 20% of orders as the test set. From the remaining training orders, we hold out a further 20% as a validation set, used only to choose model settings. Both splits are grouped by order_id, and a check confirms that no order appears on both sides of a split.

Code 
# Split by order, not by row: every item of an order goes to the same set, so the
# test score is not inflated by near-duplicate rows from the same order
set.seed(123)
split <- group_initial_split(df_model, group = order_id, prop = 0.8)
train <- training(split)
test  <- testing(split)

# Validation set: a slice of the training orders used only to choose model settings,
# so the test set stays untouched until the final scoring
inner     <- group_initial_split(train, group = order_id, prop = 0.8)
train_sub <- training(inner)
val       <- testing(inner)

leak_check <- tibble(
  check = c("Orders in both train and test", "Orders in both train-sub and validation"),
  overlapping_orders = c(
    length(intersect(train$order_id, test$order_id)),
    length(intersect(train_sub$order_id, val$order_id))
  )
)
stopifnot(all(leak_check$overlapping_orders == 0))

split_summary <- tibble(
  dataset = c("Training (sub-sample used to fit during tuning)",
              "Validation (used to choose settings)",
              "Training (full, used for final fits)",
              "Test (held out until the end)"),
  rows = c(nrow(train_sub), nrow(val), nrow(train), nrow(test)),
  orders = c(n_distinct(train_sub$order_id), n_distinct(val$order_id),
             n_distinct(train$order_id), n_distinct(test$order_id))
)

kable(split_summary, format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
      col.names = c("Dataset", "Order-item rows", "Distinct orders"),
      caption = "Grouped splits (no order appears in more than one of train / validation / test)")

The splits are random at the order level, so they test performance on similar orders from the same period. They do not test performance on future orders (see the limitations at the end).

Step 4: What the training data says about the predictors

All checks here use the training data only.

Code 
num_cor_mat <- train |>
  select(delivery_days, estimated_days, freight_value, price,
         product_weight_g, volume_cm3, ship_window_days, n_items) |>
  cor(use = "complete.obs")

corrplot(
  num_cor_mat,
  method = "color",
  type = "upper",
  addCoef.col = "black",
  number.cex = 0.7,
  tl.cex = 0.8,
  title = "Correlations among delivery_days and key numeric predictors",
  mar = c(0, 0, 2, 0)
)

Among the numeric predictors, estimated_days has the strongest linear correlation with delivery_days (r = 0.38), followed by freight_value (r = 0.21). Weight, volume, and price are only weakly correlated with delivery time on their own. Freight is moderately correlated with weight (r = 0.6) and with volume, which is why regularized models (ridge and lasso) are worth trying alongside plain linear regression.

Orders that stay within one state average 7.5 days, against 14.6 days for cross-state orders. The slowest destinations are remote northern and northeastern states, several of which have very few orders. Because of this, the recipes below do not merge small states into an “other” group; doing so would throw away exactly the states where delivery is slowest.

Step 5: Three recipes

Each recipe adds one group of predictors to the previous one. Comparing them shows what each group is worth.

Code 
# Predictor groups. Each recipe adds one group to the one before it, so the
# improvement from each group of features can be measured on its own
preds_geo <- c("customer_state", "seller_state", "same_state", "cust_region",
               "seller_region", "same_region", "purchase_year",
               "purchase_month", "purchase_dow")

preds_prod <- c("freight_value", "price", "freight_ratio", "product_weight_g",
                "volume_cm3", "density_g_cm3", "n_items", "n_sellers",
                "ship_window_days", "category", "product_photos_qty",
                "product_name_length", "product_description_length")

recipe_defs <- list(
  "R1 Geography + timing" = preds_geo,
  "R2 + Product & order"  = c(preds_geo, preds_prod),
  "R3 + Olist estimate"   = c(preds_geo, preds_prod, "estimated_days")
)

make_recipe <- function(preds) {
  rec <- recipe(delivery_days ~ .,
                data = train |> select(delivery_days, order_id, all_of(preds))) |>
    # order_id only identifies the order; it is not a predictor
    update_role(order_id, new_role = "id") |>
    # A category first seen after training gets its own level instead of causing an error
    step_novel(all_nominal_predictors())
  # Rare product categories (under 1% of rows) are pooled; states are deliberately not pooled
  # because the smallest states are the slowest destinations
  if ("category" %in% preds) rec <- rec |> step_other(category, threshold = 0.01)
  rec |>
    # Each category becomes a 0/1 indicator column
    step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
    # Drop constant columns, and columns that duplicate other columns exactly
    step_zv(all_predictors()) |>
    step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
    step_lincomb(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
    # Put every numeric predictor on the same scale so penalties treat them evenly
    step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())
}

recipe_tbl <- tibble(
  Recipe = names(recipe_defs),
  `Predictors (n)` = map_int(recipe_defs, length),
  `What it adds` = c(
    "Route (states, regions, same-state / same-region flags) and purchase timing",
    "R1 plus freight, price, weight, volume, density, order size, ship window, product category, listing quality",
    "R2 plus Olist's own checkout estimate (estimated_days)"
  )
)
kable(recipe_tbl, caption = "The three recipes")
The three recipes
Recipe Predictors (n) What it adds
R1 Geography + timing 9 Route (states, regions, same-state / same-region flags) and purchase timing
R2 + Product & order 22 R1 plus freight, price, weight, volume, density, order size, ship window, product category, listing quality
R3 + Olist estimate 23 R2 plus Olist’s own checkout estimate (estimated_days)

Every recipe applies the same preprocessing: unseen category levels are handled with step_novel(), product categories below 1% of rows are grouped (only in recipes that include category), categorical variables are dummy-encoded, constant and redundant columns are removed, missing numeric values are imputed with the median, and numeric predictors are standardized. All of it is learned from the training data inside a workflow, never from the test set.

Step 6: Benchmarks, models, and tuning

Benchmarks give the models something to beat:

  • Naive: always predict the average training delivery time.
  • Olist estimate only: a one-variable linear model on estimated_days.
  • First-draft ridge: the ridge model from the project’s first modeling iteration (freight, weight, state, and purchase month), refit on the same grouped split so the comparison is fair.

Models: linear regression (no settings), ridge and lasso (one setting each, the penalty), and a decision tree (depth and minimum node size). The penalty and tree settings are chosen as follows: fit each candidate on the training sub-sample, measure MAE on the validation set, and keep the candidate with the lowest validation MAE. The chosen settings are then refit on the full training data and scored once on the test set.

Code 
# Metrics: RMSE and MAE in days, and traditional R-squared (1 - SSE/SST)
mset <- metric_set(rmse, mae, rsq_trad)

fit_wf <- function(rec, spec, data) {
  workflow() |> add_recipe(rec) |> add_model(spec) |> fit(data)
}
# Average absolute error in days on a dataset; used to compare candidate settings
mae_on <- function(fit, data) {
  predict(fit, new_data = data) |>
    bind_cols(data |> select(delivery_days)) |>
    mae(truth = delivery_days, estimate = .pred) |>
    pull(.estimate)
}
score_fit <- function(fit) {
  predict(fit, new_data = test) |>
    bind_cols(test |> select(delivery_days)) |>
    mset(truth = delivery_days, estimate = .pred)
}

glmnet_spec <- function(p, mixture) {
  linear_reg(penalty = p, mixture = mixture) |> set_engine("glmnet")
}
# cost_complexity is fixed at a small value, so depth and minimum node size control tree complexity
tree_spec <- function(d, m) {
  decision_tree(tree_depth = d, min_n = m, cost_complexity = 0.0001) |>
    set_engine("rpart") |> set_mode("regression")
}

# Candidate settings: penalties from very weak (1e-5) to strong (1), and six tree shapes
pen_grid  <- 10^seq(-5, 0, length.out = 10)
tree_grid <- expand_grid(tree_depth = c(5, 8, 12), min_n = c(20, 60))

# Fit each candidate on the training sub-sample and keep the one with the lowest validation MAE
tune_pen <- function(rec, mixture) {
  maes <- map_dbl(pen_grid, \(p) fit_wf(rec, glmnet_spec(p, mixture), train_sub) |> mae_on(val))
  pen_grid[which.min(maes)]
}
tune_tree <- function(rec) {
  maes <- pmap_dbl(tree_grid, \(tree_depth, min_n)
                   fit_wf(rec, tree_spec(tree_depth, min_n), train_sub) |> mae_on(val))
  tree_grid[which.min(maes), ]
}

grid_tbl <- tribble(
  ~Model, ~`Setting(s) chosen on the validation set`, ~`Candidates tried`,
  "Linear regression", "None", "1",
  "Ridge (L2 penalty)", "penalty", "10 values from 1e-5 to 1",
  "Lasso (L1 penalty)", "penalty", "10 values from 1e-5 to 1",
  "Decision tree", "tree_depth, min_n", "3 depths x 2 minimum node sizes = 6"
)
kable(grid_tbl, caption = "What is tuned for each model")
What is tuned for each model
Model Setting(s) chosen on the validation set Candidates tried
Linear regression None 1
Ridge (L2 penalty) penalty 10 values from 1e-5 to 1
Lasso (L1 penalty) penalty 10 values from 1e-5 to 1

The same procedure is applied to each of the three recipes, giving twelve final models (four model families on three recipes) plus the three benchmarks.

Code 
cache_file <- "data/modeling_cache.rds"

if (file.exists(cache_file)) {
  cache <- read_rds(cache_file)
} else {
  # Benchmarks: simple reference points that every model has to beat
  bench_naive <- test |>
    mutate(.pred = mean(train$delivery_days)) |>
    mset(truth = delivery_days, estimate = .pred) |>
    mutate(recipe = "Benchmark", model = "Naive (train mean)", settings = "")

  fit_olist <- fit_wf(recipe(delivery_days ~ estimated_days, data = train),
                      linear_reg() |> set_engine("lm"), train)
  bench_olist <- score_fit(fit_olist) |>
    mutate(recipe = "Benchmark", model = "Olist estimate only (LM)", settings = "")

  # First-draft model: the original small feature set, refit on the same grouped split
  rec_orig <- recipe(delivery_days ~ freight_value + product_weight_g +
                       customer_state + seller_state + purchase_month,
                     data = train) |>
    step_other(all_nominal_predictors(), threshold = 0.02) |>
    step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
    step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())
  fit_orig <- fit_wf(rec_orig, glmnet_spec(0.1, 0), train)
  bench_orig <- score_fit(fit_orig) |>
    mutate(recipe = "Benchmark", model = "First-draft ridge (original features)",
           settings = "penalty=0.1")

  # Fit all four model families on each recipe. Settings are chosen on the validation set,
  # then the final models are refit on the full training data
  run_recipe <- function(preds, rec_name) {
    rec   <- make_recipe(preds)
    pen_r <- tune_pen(rec, 0)
    pen_l <- tune_pen(rec, 1)
    bt    <- tune_tree(rec)

    fits <- list(
      "Linear Regression" = fit_wf(rec, linear_reg() |> set_engine("lm"), train),
      "Ridge"             = fit_wf(rec, glmnet_spec(pen_r, 0), train),
      "Lasso"             = fit_wf(rec, glmnet_spec(pen_l, 1), train),
      "Decision Tree"     = fit_wf(rec, tree_spec(bt$tree_depth, bt$min_n), train)
    )
    settings <- c(
      "Linear Regression" = "none",
      "Ridge"             = paste0("penalty=", signif(pen_r, 2)),
      "Lasso"             = paste0("penalty=", signif(pen_l, 2)),
      "Decision Tree"     = paste0("depth=", bt$tree_depth, ", min_n=", bt$min_n)
    )

    list(
      metrics = imap(fits, \(fit, model_name)
                     score_fit(fit) |>
                       mutate(recipe = rec_name, model = model_name,
                              settings = settings[[model_name]])) |>
        list_rbind(),
      fits = fits[c("Lasso", "Decision Tree")]
    )
  }

  runs <- imap(recipe_defs, run_recipe)

  cache <- list(
    results_all = bind_rows(bench_naive, bench_olist, bench_orig,
                            map(runs, "metrics") |> list_rbind()),
    fit_lasso3  = runs[["R3 + Olist estimate"]]$fits[["Lasso"]],
    fit_tree3   = runs[["R3 + Olist estimate"]]$fits[["Decision Tree"]]
  )
  write_rds(cache, cache_file)
}

results_all <- cache$results_all
fit_lasso3  <- cache$fit_lasso3
fit_tree3   <- cache$fit_tree3

Step 7: Test-set comparison

All numbers below are measured on the held-out test set, in days.

Code 
results_wide <- results_all |>

  pivot_wider(names_from = .metric, values_from = .estimate) |>
  arrange(mae)

Key takeaways from the model comparison

  1. Best configuration: Decision Tree on R3 + Olist estimate, with a test MAE of 4.79 days, RMSE of 7.61 days, and R² of 0.31. In plain terms, using only information available at checkout, the model explains about 31% of the variation in delivery time, with a typical miss of about 4.8 days.
  2. Improvement over the benchmarks: MAE is 24% lower than always predicting the average (6.31 days), and 9% lower than the first-draft ridge (5.25 days; R² 0.24) on the same grouped split.
  3. Features matter more than model choice. For linear regression, adding product and order features (R1 to R2) lowers MAE from 5.01 to 4.87 days. Adding Olist’s own estimate (R2 to R3) lowers it only to 4.85 days. That estimate is weak on its own (R² of 0.15), and most of what it knows about the route is already captured by the state and region features.
  4. Regularization made almost no difference. In Recipe 3, linear regression, ridge, and lasso have RMSEs between 7.59 and 7.6 days. With about 88,157 training rows and a modest number of predictors, there is little overfitting for a penalty to fix. Differences this small are within the noise of a single test split.
  5. The tree is close to the linear models, not far ahead. In Recipe 3 the decision tree’s MAE is 4.79 days against 4.85 for linear regression, a gap of 0.06 days. Its RMSE (7.61) is slightly worse than linear regression’s (7.59), which suggests the tree does not handle the longest delays any better.
  6. RMSE is much larger than MAE (7.6 vs 4.8 days): most orders are predicted well, but a minority of very late orders produce large errors. The diagnostics below look at this directly.

Step 8: Diagnostics for the decision tree (Recipe 3)

We use the decision tree for diagnostics because it has the lowest MAE in the comparison. We use the lasso in the next step because its coefficients are easier to interpret.

  bind_cols(test) |>
  # Residual = actual minus predicted days; positive means the order took longer than predicted
  mutate(residual = delivery_days - .pred)

# Share of test orders whose prediction is within +/- N days of the actual delivery time
band_tbl <- tibble(window_days = c(2, 3, 5, 7, 10)) |>
  mutate(share = map_dbl(window_days, \(w) mean(abs(test_preds$residual) <= w)))

kable(

  col.names = c("Prediction within +/- this many days", "Share of test orders"),

Key takeaways from the diagnostics

  • Most predictions are close. About 68% of test orders land within 5 days of the prediction, and 90% within 10 days.
  • The misses are lopsided. The model under-predicts by more than 10 days on 7.0% of orders, but over-predicts by more than 10 days on only 3.2%. Because the model predicts a typical value for a right-skewed target, the very slow orders are the ones it misses.
  • Error depends on where the order goes. Among states with enough test orders, MAE is highest for CE and lowest for SP.
  • Practical implication: a single predicted number is a good guide for typical orders, but it should be paired with a buffer for long routes and for the slow months, instead of being promised to the customer as exact.

Step 9: What drives the predictions?

Lasso coefficients

The lasso shrinks the coefficients of unhelpful predictors to exactly zero, so the features that survive are the ones the model finds useful. Predictors are standardized, so each coefficient is the change in predicted delivery days for a one-standard-deviation increase in that predictor (for a dummy variable, a one-standard-deviation change in the 0/1 indicator). Coefficients show direction and relative size, not causal effects.

Code 
# Coefficients are per one standard deviation of each predictor; zero means the lasso dropped it
lasso_coefs <- tidy(fit_lasso3) |> filter(term != "(Intercept)")
n_kept  <- sum(lasso_coefs$estimate != 0)
n_total <- nrow(lasso_coefs)

top_coefs <- lasso_coefs |>
  filter(estimate != 0) |>
  slice_max(abs(estimate), n = 15) |>
  mutate(direction = if_else(estimate > 0, "Slower delivery", "Faster delivery"))

ggplot(top_coefs, aes(x = estimate, y = reorder(term, estimate), fill = direction)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Slower delivery" = "#d95f02", "Faster delivery" = "#1b9e77")) +
  labs(
    title = "Lasso: largest coefficients",
    x = "Change in predicted delivery days per 1 SD of the predictor",
    y = NULL, fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

The lasso kept 109 of 112 encoded predictors.

Decision tree importance, grouped by original feature

A tree’s raw importance scores are split across dummy columns, so a feature like customer_state appears as 27 small bars. We add the scores back together by original feature to get a clearer picture.

Code 
imp <- extract_fit_engine(fit_tree3)$variable.importance

imp_tbl <- tibble(term = names(imp), importance = imp) |>
  # A feature such as customer_state is split into many dummy columns; add them back together
  mutate(feature = case_when(
    str_detect(term, "^customer_state") ~ "customer_state",
    str_detect(term, "^seller_state")   ~ "seller_state",
    str_detect(term, "^same_state")     ~ "same_state",
    str_detect(term, "^same_region")    ~ "same_region",
    str_detect(term, "^cust_region")    ~ "customer_zip_region",
    str_detect(term, "^seller_region")  ~ "seller_zip_region",
    str_detect(term, "^purchase_year")  ~ "purchase_year",
    str_detect(term, "^purchase_month") ~ "purchase_month",
    str_detect(term, "^purchase_dow")   ~ "purchase_weekday",
    str_detect(term, "^category")       ~ "product_category",
    TRUE ~ term
  )) |>
  group_by(feature) |>
  summarise(importance = sum(importance), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(share = importance / sum(importance)) |>
  arrange(desc(importance))

imp_tbl |>
  slice_head(n = 12) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = share, y = reorder(feature, share))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2b8cbe") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(
    title = "Decision tree: share of importance by feature (Recipe 3)",
    x = "Share of total importance", y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

Key takeaways on drivers

  • Route features dominate. The three most important feature groups in the tree are customer_state (18%), same_state (17%), and estimated_days (14%). Where an item travels from and to is the strongest driver of delivery time.
  • Purchase timing contributes a smaller share (10% for year, month, and weekday combined), consistent with the exploration page’s finding that purchase timing barely changes delivery outcomes. The months that do show up match the slow months seen in the exploration.
  • estimated_days ranks high in importance but added little to accuracy. The tree uses it often, but because route features carry much of the same information, removing it costs little. Importance measures how much a feature is used; the recipe comparison measures how much accuracy it adds.
  • Caution: correlated features share credit in tree importance, and neither the lasso nor the tree shows causation. These results describe what the models rely on to predict, not what causes a delay.

Key Takeaways and Limitations

What we found

  • Delivery time on Olist is driven mainly by route (seller and customer location), with product and order characteristics adding a smaller amount and purchase timing adding little.
  • The best model (Decision Tree, R3 + Olist estimate) predicts delivery time to within about 4.8 days on average and explains about 31% of the variation, improving MAE by 9% over the first draft and 24% over the naive average.
  • Model choice mattered far less than feature choice: ridge, lasso, and linear regression perform almost identically, and the decision tree is only slightly different.
  • Olist’s own estimate carries limited extra information once route features are present, which supports the earlier finding that the estimates are conservative rather than precise.

How far to trust it

  • Single random split. All results come from one test set. Differences of a few hundredths of a day between models are not meaningful, and a different random split would shift the numbers slightly.
  • Similar orders, not future orders. The split is random across 2016-2018, so it tests performance on orders like those already seen. It does not test how the model would perform after a carrier change, a strike, or a seasonal shift.
  • Tail delays are still hard. The model tends to under-predict the slowest orders, so a point estimate should be paired with a delivery window.
  • Order-item grain. delivery_days is an order-level duration repeated across the items of an order, so multi-item orders carry slightly more weight in the metrics.
  • Settings chosen on one validation slice. Tuning used a single validation set. If a chosen setting sits at the edge of its search grid (see the Settings column), a wider search might change results slightly.
  • Interpretation of coefficients. Standardized lasso coefficients show direction and relative size, not causal effects.
  • Unmeasured factors. Carrier performance, weather, seller behavior, and true seller-to-customer distance are not in the data. Zip-code region is only a coarse stand-in for distance.

What could improve it

Adding real seller-to-customer distance (from Olist’s geolocation table) is the most promising next step. Non-linear ensemble models or a log-transformed target are further options that were outside the scope of this analysis.

# Overview and Target / Leakage Guardrails

This analysis builds models that predict `delivery_days` (days from order purchase to customer delivery) using only information that is available when an order is placed or approved. It starts from the cleaned order-item dataset prepared on the Data page, engineers route, product, and timing features, and compares **three feature recipes** across **four model families**, plus benchmarks, on a held-out test set.

**Design choices**

- **Split by order, not by row.** The data has one row per order *item*, and `delivery_days` repeats across the items of an order. If items from one order landed in both training and test data, the test score would be inflated. Every split below keeps all items of an order together.
- **Train / validation / test, no cross-validation.** Model settings are chosen on a validation set carved out of the training data. The test set is used once, at the end.
- **Three recipes that add one group of features at a time**, so we can see what each group contributes.
- **Four model families:** linear regression, ridge, lasso, and a decision tree.
- **Metrics in days.** We keep `delivery_days` on its raw scale so errors are directly interpretable. MAE (average absolute error) is the primary metric, RMSE (which penalizes large misses more) is secondary, and R² is the traditional version, `1 - SSE/SST` on the test set. An R² of 0 means no better than predicting the average; it can be negative.

**What was kept out of the predictors, and why**

```{r}
#| label: leakage-table
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(corrplot)
library(knitr)
tidymodels_prefer()

leakage_tbl <- tribble(
  ~Field, ~Treatment, ~Reason,
  "delivery_days, order_delivered_customer_date", "Target / outcome", "Only known after delivery",
  "delayed_days, delivered_status", "Excluded", "Derived from the target",
  "order_status", "Excluded", "Recorded after the order is placed",
  "order_estimated_delivery_date", "Used only as estimated_days (Recipe 3)", "Olist's estimate, shown at checkout",
  "shipping_limit_date", "Used only as ship_window_days", "Seller deadline, assumed known at order approval",
  "order_purchase_timestamp", "Used as year, month, weekday", "Known at purchase",
  "order_id", "Grouping only", "Keeps items of one order in the same split",
  "customer_id, customer_unique_id, product_id, seller_id", "Excluded", "Identifiers with thousands of levels",
  "City names, full zip prefixes", "Excluded (first zip digit used as a coarse region)", "Too many levels to model reliably"
)

kable(leakage_tbl, caption = "Fields excluded or restricted to avoid leakage")
```

## Step 1: Checking skewness of `delivery_days`

Before splitting, we compare the mean, median, and the `log10(delivery_days)` histogram to see whether the target is right-skewed. The `log10` histogram excludes zero-day rows because $\log_{10}(0)$ is undefined.

```{r}
#| label: skew-check
df_clean <- read_rds("data/df_master_clean.rds")

skew_check_tbl <- df_clean |>
  summarise(
    min_days = min(delivery_days),
    n_zero_days = sum(delivery_days == 0),
    mean_days = mean(delivery_days),
    median_days = median(delivery_days),
    max_days = max(delivery_days),
    sd_days = sd(delivery_days),
    n_rows = n()
  )

kable(
  skew_check_tbl,
  digits = 2,
  format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
  col.names = c("Min", "Zero-Day Rows", "Mean", "Median", "Max", "SD", "Rows"),
  caption = "Skewness check on delivery_days before splitting"
)
```

```{r}
#| label: skew-plot
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of positive delivery_days on a base-10 log scale"
#| fig-height: 3.5
ggplot(df_clean |> filter(delivery_days > 0), aes(x = log10(delivery_days))) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "#1b9e77", color = "white", alpha = 0.9) +
  labs(
    title = "log10(delivery_days) pulls in the right tail",
    subtitle = "Zero-day rows excluded from this chart only",
    x = "log10(delivery_days)",
    y = "Order-item count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Across the `r format(skew_check_tbl$n_rows, big.mark = ",")` cleaned order-item rows, `delivery_days` is right-skewed: the mean (`r round(skew_check_tbl$mean_days, 2)` days) exceeds the median (`r skew_check_tbl$median_days` days), the standard deviation is `r round(skew_check_tbl$sd_days, 2)` days, and the tail reaches `r skew_check_tbl$max_days` days. A log transform would make the distribution more symmetric, but we keep the raw scale so that MAE and RMSE stay directly interpretable in days for a logistics manager.

## Step 2: Feature engineering

We build features in four groups: route (where the item travels), timing, product and order characteristics, and Olist's own checkout estimate.

```{r}
#| label: feature-engineering
df_model <- df_clean |>
  # Order size: how many items, and how many different sellers, share one order
  group_by(order_id) |>
  mutate(n_items = n(), n_sellers = n_distinct(seller_id)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(
    # Handling time the seller was given before the item had to ship
    ship_window_days = as.numeric(difftime(shipping_limit_date,
                                           order_purchase_timestamp, units = "days")),
    # Package size, density, and shipping cost relative to item value
    volume_cm3    = product_length_cm * product_height_cm * product_width_cm,
    density_g_cm3 = product_weight_g / pmax(volume_cm3, 1),
    freight_ratio = freight_value / price,
    # Route features. Coordinates are not available, so distance is approximated by a
    # same-state flag and by the first digit of the zip prefix (a coarse geographic region)
    same_state    = factor(if_else(seller_state == customer_state, "same", "different")),
    cust_region   = factor(substr(sprintf("%05d", as.integer(customer_zip_code_prefix)), 1, 1)),
    seller_region = factor(substr(sprintf("%05d", as.integer(seller_zip_code_prefix)), 1, 1)),
    same_region   = factor(if_else(cust_region == seller_region, "same", "different")),
    # Timing and category fields are treated as categories, because seasonality
    # (for example a slow month) is not a straight-line effect
    purchase_year  = factor(purchase_year),
    purchase_month = factor(purchase_month),
    purchase_dow   = factor(purchase_day_of_week),
    customer_state = factor(customer_state),
    seller_state   = factor(seller_state),
    category       = factor(product_category_name_english)
  ) |>
  select(order_id, delivery_days, estimated_days,
         customer_state, seller_state, same_state, cust_region, seller_region,
         same_region, purchase_year, purchase_month, purchase_dow,
         freight_value, price, freight_ratio, product_weight_g, volume_cm3,
         density_g_cm3, n_items, n_sellers, ship_window_days, category,
         product_photos_qty, product_name_length, product_description_length)
```

```{r}
#| label: feature-table
feature_tbl <- tribble(
  ~Feature, ~`Built from`, ~`Why it might matter`,

  "cust_region, seller_region", "First digit of the 5-digit zip prefix (a coarse region, since postal codes are assigned roughly by geography)", "Stand-in for distance without needing coordinates",
  "purchase_year, purchase_month, purchase_dow", "Purchase timestamp", "Seasonality, plus partial years (2016 and 2018) in the data",
  "volume_cm3, density_g_cm3", "Length x height x width; weight / volume", "Bulky or dense items may ship differently",
  "freight_ratio", "Freight / price", "Shipping cost relative to item value",
  "n_items, n_sellers", "Rows and distinct sellers within an order", "Multi-seller orders may take longer",
  "ship_window_days", "Shipping deadline minus purchase time", "How much handling time the seller was given",
  "estimated_days", "Olist's estimated delivery date minus purchase date", "Olist's own prediction, known at checkout"
)

kable(feature_tbl, caption = "Engineered features and the reason for including them")
```

## Step 3: Train / validation / test split, grouped by order

We hold out 20% of orders as the test set. From the remaining training orders, we hold out a further 20% as a validation set, used only to choose model settings. Both splits are grouped by `order_id`, and a check confirms that no order appears on both sides of a split.

```{r}
#| label: split
# Split by order, not by row: every item of an order goes to the same set, so the
# test score is not inflated by near-duplicate rows from the same order
set.seed(123)
split <- group_initial_split(df_model, group = order_id, prop = 0.8)
train <- training(split)
test  <- testing(split)

# Validation set: a slice of the training orders used only to choose model settings,
# so the test set stays untouched until the final scoring
inner     <- group_initial_split(train, group = order_id, prop = 0.8)
train_sub <- training(inner)
val       <- testing(inner)

leak_check <- tibble(
  check = c("Orders in both train and test", "Orders in both train-sub and validation"),
  overlapping_orders = c(
    length(intersect(train$order_id, test$order_id)),
    length(intersect(train_sub$order_id, val$order_id))
  )
)
stopifnot(all(leak_check$overlapping_orders == 0))

split_summary <- tibble(
  dataset = c("Training (sub-sample used to fit during tuning)",
              "Validation (used to choose settings)",
              "Training (full, used for final fits)",
              "Test (held out until the end)"),
  rows = c(nrow(train_sub), nrow(val), nrow(train), nrow(test)),
  orders = c(n_distinct(train_sub$order_id), n_distinct(val$order_id),
             n_distinct(train$order_id), n_distinct(test$order_id))
)

kable(split_summary, format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
      col.names = c("Dataset", "Order-item rows", "Distinct orders"),
      caption = "Grouped splits (no order appears in more than one of train / validation / test)")
kable(leak_check, col.names = c("Leakage check", "Overlapping orders"),
      caption = "Leakage check: both must be zero")
```

The splits are random at the order level, so they test performance on *similar* orders from the same period. They do not test performance on future orders (see the limitations at the end).

## Step 4: What the training data says about the predictors

All checks here use the training data only.

```{r}
#| label: correlations
#| fig-cap: "Correlations among delivery_days and key numeric predictors (training data)"
#| fig-height: 5
num_cor_mat <- train |>
  select(delivery_days, estimated_days, freight_value, price,
         product_weight_g, volume_cm3, ship_window_days, n_items) |>
  cor(use = "complete.obs")

corrplot(
  num_cor_mat,
  method = "color",
  type = "upper",
  addCoef.col = "black",
  number.cex = 0.7,
  tl.cex = 0.8,
  title = "Correlations among delivery_days and key numeric predictors",
  mar = c(0, 0, 2, 0)
)
```

Among the numeric predictors, `estimated_days` has the strongest linear correlation with `delivery_days` (r = `r round(num_cor_mat["delivery_days", "estimated_days"], 2)`), followed by `freight_value` (r = `r round(num_cor_mat["delivery_days", "freight_value"], 2)`). Weight, volume, and price are only weakly correlated with delivery time on their own. Freight is moderately correlated with weight (r = `r round(num_cor_mat["freight_value", "product_weight_g"], 2)`) and with volume, which is why regularized models (ridge and lasso) are worth trying alongside plain linear regression.

```{r}
  head(cat_state_summary, 10),
  digits = 2,
  format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
  col.names = c("Customer state", "Training rows", "Mean days", "Median days"),
  caption = "Ten slowest customer states by mean delivery_days (training data)"
)
```

Orders that stay within one state average `r round(route_summary$mean_days[route_summary$same_state == "same"], 1)` days, against `r round(route_summary$mean_days[route_summary$same_state == "different"], 1)` days for cross-state orders. The slowest destinations are remote northern and northeastern states, several of which have very few orders. Because of this, the recipes below do **not** merge small states into an "other" group; doing so would throw away exactly the states where delivery is slowest.

## Step 5: Three recipes

Each recipe adds one group of predictors to the previous one. Comparing them shows what each group is worth.

```{r}
#| label: recipes
# Predictor groups. Each recipe adds one group to the one before it, so the
# improvement from each group of features can be measured on its own
preds_geo <- c("customer_state", "seller_state", "same_state", "cust_region",
               "seller_region", "same_region", "purchase_year",
               "purchase_month", "purchase_dow")

preds_prod <- c("freight_value", "price", "freight_ratio", "product_weight_g",
                "volume_cm3", "density_g_cm3", "n_items", "n_sellers",
                "ship_window_days", "category", "product_photos_qty",
                "product_name_length", "product_description_length")

recipe_defs <- list(
  "R1 Geography + timing" = preds_geo,
  "R2 + Product & order"  = c(preds_geo, preds_prod),
  "R3 + Olist estimate"   = c(preds_geo, preds_prod, "estimated_days")
)

make_recipe <- function(preds) {
  rec <- recipe(delivery_days ~ .,
                data = train |> select(delivery_days, order_id, all_of(preds))) |>
    # order_id only identifies the order; it is not a predictor
    update_role(order_id, new_role = "id") |>
    # A category first seen after training gets its own level instead of causing an error
    step_novel(all_nominal_predictors())
  # Rare product categories (under 1% of rows) are pooled; states are deliberately not pooled
  # because the smallest states are the slowest destinations
  if ("category" %in% preds) rec <- rec |> step_other(category, threshold = 0.01)
  rec |>
    # Each category becomes a 0/1 indicator column
    step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
    # Drop constant columns, and columns that duplicate other columns exactly
    step_zv(all_predictors()) |>
    step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
    step_lincomb(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
    # Put every numeric predictor on the same scale so penalties treat them evenly
    step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())
}

recipe_tbl <- tibble(
  Recipe = names(recipe_defs),
  `Predictors (n)` = map_int(recipe_defs, length),
  `What it adds` = c(
    "Route (states, regions, same-state / same-region flags) and purchase timing",
    "R1 plus freight, price, weight, volume, density, order size, ship window, product category, listing quality",
    "R2 plus Olist's own checkout estimate (estimated_days)"
  )
)
kable(recipe_tbl, caption = "The three recipes")
```

Every recipe applies the same preprocessing: unseen category levels are handled with `step_novel()`, product categories below 1% of rows are grouped (only in recipes that include `category`), categorical variables are dummy-encoded, constant and redundant columns are removed, missing numeric values are imputed with the median, and numeric predictors are standardized. All of it is learned from the training data inside a `workflow`, never from the test set.

## Step 6: Benchmarks, models, and tuning

**Benchmarks** give the models something to beat:

- **Naive:** always predict the average training delivery time.
- **Olist estimate only:** a one-variable linear model on `estimated_days`.
- **First-draft ridge:** the ridge model from the project's first modeling iteration (freight, weight, state, and purchase month), refit on the same grouped split so the comparison is fair.

**Models:** linear regression (no settings), ridge and lasso (one setting each, the penalty), and a decision tree (depth and minimum node size). The penalty and tree settings are chosen as follows: fit each candidate on the training sub-sample, measure MAE on the validation set, and keep the candidate with the lowest validation MAE. The chosen settings are then refit on the full training data and scored once on the test set.

```{r}
#| label: helpers
# Metrics: RMSE and MAE in days, and traditional R-squared (1 - SSE/SST)
mset <- metric_set(rmse, mae, rsq_trad)

fit_wf <- function(rec, spec, data) {
  workflow() |> add_recipe(rec) |> add_model(spec) |> fit(data)
}
# Average absolute error in days on a dataset; used to compare candidate settings
mae_on <- function(fit, data) {
  predict(fit, new_data = data) |>
    bind_cols(data |> select(delivery_days)) |>
    mae(truth = delivery_days, estimate = .pred) |>
    pull(.estimate)
}
score_fit <- function(fit) {
  predict(fit, new_data = test) |>
    bind_cols(test |> select(delivery_days)) |>
    mset(truth = delivery_days, estimate = .pred)
}

glmnet_spec <- function(p, mixture) {
  linear_reg(penalty = p, mixture = mixture) |> set_engine("glmnet")
}
# cost_complexity is fixed at a small value, so depth and minimum node size control tree complexity
tree_spec <- function(d, m) {
  decision_tree(tree_depth = d, min_n = m, cost_complexity = 0.0001) |>
    set_engine("rpart") |> set_mode("regression")
}

# Candidate settings: penalties from very weak (1e-5) to strong (1), and six tree shapes
pen_grid  <- 10^seq(-5, 0, length.out = 10)
tree_grid <- expand_grid(tree_depth = c(5, 8, 12), min_n = c(20, 60))

# Fit each candidate on the training sub-sample and keep the one with the lowest validation MAE
tune_pen <- function(rec, mixture) {
  maes <- map_dbl(pen_grid, \(p) fit_wf(rec, glmnet_spec(p, mixture), train_sub) |> mae_on(val))
  pen_grid[which.min(maes)]
}
tune_tree <- function(rec) {
  maes <- pmap_dbl(tree_grid, \(tree_depth, min_n)
                   fit_wf(rec, tree_spec(tree_depth, min_n), train_sub) |> mae_on(val))
  tree_grid[which.min(maes), ]
}

grid_tbl <- tribble(
  ~Model, ~`Setting(s) chosen on the validation set`, ~`Candidates tried`,
  "Linear regression", "None", "1",
  "Ridge (L2 penalty)", "penalty", "10 values from 1e-5 to 1",
  "Lasso (L1 penalty)", "penalty", "10 values from 1e-5 to 1",
  "Decision tree", "tree_depth, min_n", "3 depths x 2 minimum node sizes = 6"
)
kable(grid_tbl, caption = "What is tuned for each model")
```

The same procedure is applied to each of the three recipes, giving twelve final models (four model families on three recipes) plus the three benchmarks.

```{r}
#| label: fit-models
cache_file <- "data/modeling_cache.rds"

if (file.exists(cache_file)) {
  cache <- read_rds(cache_file)
} else {
  # Benchmarks: simple reference points that every model has to beat
  bench_naive <- test |>
    mutate(.pred = mean(train$delivery_days)) |>
    mset(truth = delivery_days, estimate = .pred) |>
    mutate(recipe = "Benchmark", model = "Naive (train mean)", settings = "")

  fit_olist <- fit_wf(recipe(delivery_days ~ estimated_days, data = train),
                      linear_reg() |> set_engine("lm"), train)
  bench_olist <- score_fit(fit_olist) |>
    mutate(recipe = "Benchmark", model = "Olist estimate only (LM)", settings = "")

  # First-draft model: the original small feature set, refit on the same grouped split
  rec_orig <- recipe(delivery_days ~ freight_value + product_weight_g +
                       customer_state + seller_state + purchase_month,
                     data = train) |>
    step_other(all_nominal_predictors(), threshold = 0.02) |>
    step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
    step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())
  fit_orig <- fit_wf(rec_orig, glmnet_spec(0.1, 0), train)
  bench_orig <- score_fit(fit_orig) |>
    mutate(recipe = "Benchmark", model = "First-draft ridge (original features)",
           settings = "penalty=0.1")

  # Fit all four model families on each recipe. Settings are chosen on the validation set,
  # then the final models are refit on the full training data
  run_recipe <- function(preds, rec_name) {
    rec   <- make_recipe(preds)
    pen_r <- tune_pen(rec, 0)
    pen_l <- tune_pen(rec, 1)
    bt    <- tune_tree(rec)

    fits <- list(
      "Linear Regression" = fit_wf(rec, linear_reg() |> set_engine("lm"), train),
      "Ridge"             = fit_wf(rec, glmnet_spec(pen_r, 0), train),
      "Lasso"             = fit_wf(rec, glmnet_spec(pen_l, 1), train),
      "Decision Tree"     = fit_wf(rec, tree_spec(bt$tree_depth, bt$min_n), train)
    )
    settings <- c(
      "Linear Regression" = "none",
      "Ridge"             = paste0("penalty=", signif(pen_r, 2)),
      "Lasso"             = paste0("penalty=", signif(pen_l, 2)),
      "Decision Tree"     = paste0("depth=", bt$tree_depth, ", min_n=", bt$min_n)
    )

    list(
      metrics = imap(fits, \(fit, model_name)
                     score_fit(fit) |>
                       mutate(recipe = rec_name, model = model_name,
                              settings = settings[[model_name]])) |>
        list_rbind(),
      fits = fits[c("Lasso", "Decision Tree")]
    )
  }

  runs <- imap(recipe_defs, run_recipe)

  cache <- list(
    results_all = bind_rows(bench_naive, bench_olist, bench_orig,
                            map(runs, "metrics") |> list_rbind()),
    fit_lasso3  = runs[["R3 + Olist estimate"]]$fits[["Lasso"]],
    fit_tree3   = runs[["R3 + Olist estimate"]]$fits[["Decision Tree"]]
  )
  write_rds(cache, cache_file)
}

results_all <- cache$results_all
fit_lasso3  <- cache$fit_lasso3
fit_tree3   <- cache$fit_tree3
```

All numbers below are measured on the held-out test set, in days.

```{r}
kable(
```

```{r}
#| label: takeaway-values
#| include: false
get_metric <- function(rec, mod, met) {
  results_all |> filter(recipe == rec, model == mod, .metric == met) |> pull(.estimate)
}
r1 <- names(recipe_defs)[1]; r2 <- names(recipe_defs)[2]; r3 <- names(recipe_defs)[3]

best_row <- results_wide |>
  filter(recipe != "Benchmark") |>
  slice_min(mae, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)

naive_mae  <- get_metric("Benchmark", "Naive (train mean)", "mae")
naive_rmse <- get_metric("Benchmark", "Naive (train mean)", "rmse")
olist_r2   <- get_metric("Benchmark", "Olist estimate only (LM)", "rsq_trad")
draft_mae  <- get_metric("Benchmark", "First-draft ridge (original features)", "mae")
draft_r2   <- get_metric("Benchmark", "First-draft ridge (original features)", "rsq_trad")

lm_r1_mae <- get_metric(r1, "Linear Regression", "mae")
lm_r2_mae <- get_metric(r2, "Linear Regression", "mae")
lm_r3_mae <- get_metric(r3, "Linear Regression", "mae")

r3_rmse_range <- results_all |>
  filter(recipe == r3, .metric == "rmse", model %in% c("Linear Regression", "Ridge", "Lasso")) |>
  pull(.estimate) |> range()

tree_r3_mae <- get_metric(r3, "Decision Tree", "mae")
tree_r3_rmse <- get_metric(r3, "Decision Tree", "rmse")
lin_r3_rmse <- get_metric(r3, "Linear Regression", "rmse")
```

### Key takeaways from the model comparison

1. **Best configuration:** `r best_row$model` on `r best_row$recipe`, with a test MAE of `r round(best_row$mae, 2)` days, RMSE of `r round(best_row$rmse, 2)` days, and R² of `r round(best_row$rsq_trad, 2)`. In plain terms, using only information available at checkout, the model explains about `r round(100 * best_row$rsq_trad)`% of the variation in delivery time, with a typical miss of about `r round(best_row$mae, 1)` days.
2. **Improvement over the benchmarks:** MAE is `r round(100 * (1 - best_row$mae / naive_mae))`% lower than always predicting the average (`r round(naive_mae, 2)` days), and `r round(100 * (1 - best_row$mae / draft_mae))`% lower than the first-draft ridge (`r round(draft_mae, 2)` days; R² `r round(draft_r2, 2)`) on the same grouped split.
3. **Features matter more than model choice.** For linear regression, adding product and order features (R1 to R2) lowers MAE from `r round(lm_r1_mae, 2)` to `r round(lm_r2_mae, 2)` days. Adding Olist's own estimate (R2 to R3) lowers it only to `r round(lm_r3_mae, 2)` days. That estimate is weak on its own (R² of `r round(olist_r2, 2)`), and most of what it knows about the route is already captured by the state and region features.
4. **Regularization made almost no difference.** In Recipe 3, linear regression, ridge, and lasso have RMSEs between `r round(r3_rmse_range[1], 2)` and `r round(r3_rmse_range[2], 2)` days. With about `r format(nrow(train), big.mark = ",")` training rows and a modest number of predictors, there is little overfitting for a penalty to fix. Differences this small are within the noise of a single test split.
5. **The tree is close to the linear models, not far ahead.** In Recipe 3 the decision tree's MAE is `r round(tree_r3_mae, 2)` days against `r round(lm_r3_mae, 2)` for linear regression, a gap of `r round(abs(tree_r3_mae - lm_r3_mae), 2)` days. Its RMSE (`r round(tree_r3_rmse, 2)`) is `r if (tree_r3_rmse > lin_r3_rmse) "slightly worse" else "slightly better"` than linear regression's (`r round(lin_r3_rmse, 2)`), which suggests the tree does not handle the longest delays any better.
6. **RMSE is much larger than MAE** (`r round(best_row$rmse, 1)` vs `r round(best_row$mae, 1)` days): most orders are predicted well, but a minority of very late orders produce large errors. The diagnostics below look at this directly.

## Step 8: Diagnostics for the decision tree (Recipe 3)

We use the decision tree for diagnostics because it has the lowest MAE in the comparison. We use the lasso in the next step because its coefficients are easier to interpret.

```{r}
#| label: diagnostics-data
test_preds <- predict(fit_tree3, new_data = test) |>
  bind_cols(test) |>
  # Residual = actual minus predicted days; positive means the order took longer than predicted
  mutate(residual = delivery_days - .pred)

# Share of test orders whose prediction is within +/- N days of the actual delivery time
band_tbl <- tibble(window_days = c(2, 3, 5, 7, 10)) |>
  mutate(share = map_dbl(window_days, \(w) mean(abs(test_preds$residual) <= w)))

kable(
  band_tbl |> mutate(share = scales::percent(share, accuracy = 0.1)),
  col.names = c("Prediction within +/- this many days", "Share of test orders"),
  caption = "How often the prediction lands close to the actual delivery time"
)
```

```{r}
#| label: pred-vs-actual
#| fig-cap: "Predicted vs. actual delivery days (test set, decision tree, Recipe 3)"
#| fig-height: 4.5
ggplot(test_preds, aes(x = delivery_days, y = .pred)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2, color = "#2b8cbe") +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "#d95f02", linewidth = 0.9) +
  labs(
    title = "Predicted vs. actual delivery days",
    subtitle = "Points below the dashed line are under-predictions of slow orders",
    x = "Actual delivery_days (test set)",
    y = "Predicted delivery_days"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
#| label: residuals
#| fig-cap: "Residuals vs. predicted delivery days (test set, decision tree, Recipe 3)"
#| fig-height: 4.5
ggplot(test_preds, aes(x = .pred, y = residual)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2, color = "#2b8cbe") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "#d95f02", linewidth = 0.9) +
  labs(
    title = "Residuals vs. predicted delivery days",
    subtitle = "Positive residuals: the order took longer than predicted",
    x = "Predicted delivery_days",
    y = "Residual (actual - predicted days)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
#| label: error-by-state
#| fig-cap: "Test MAE by customer state (states with at least 200 test rows)"
#| fig-height: 5
state_err <- test_preds |>
  group_by(customer_state) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mae = mean(abs(residual)), bias = mean(residual), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(n >= 200) |>
  arrange(desc(mae))

ggplot(state_err, aes(x = mae, y = reorder(customer_state, mae))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2b8cbe") +
  labs(
    title = "Prediction error is largest for remote destination states",
    x = "Test MAE (days)", y = "Customer state"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
#| label: diagnostics-values
#| include: false
under_10 <- mean(test_preds$residual > 10)
over_10  <- mean(test_preds$residual < -10)
within_5 <- band_tbl$share[band_tbl$window_days == 5]
within_10 <- band_tbl$share[band_tbl$window_days == 10]
worst_state <- state_err$customer_state[1]
best_state  <- state_err$customer_state[nrow(state_err)]
```

### Key takeaways from the diagnostics

- **Most predictions are close.** About `r scales::percent(within_5, accuracy = 1)` of test orders land within 5 days of the prediction, and `r scales::percent(within_10, accuracy = 1)` within 10 days.
- **The misses are lopsided.** The model under-predicts by more than 10 days on `r scales::percent(under_10, accuracy = 0.1)` of orders, but over-predicts by more than 10 days on only `r scales::percent(over_10, accuracy = 0.1)`. Because the model predicts a typical value for a right-skewed target, the very slow orders are the ones it misses.
- **Error depends on where the order goes.** Among states with enough test orders, MAE is highest for `r worst_state` and lowest for `r best_state`.
- **Practical implication:** a single predicted number is a good guide for typical orders, but it should be paired with a buffer for long routes and for the slow months, instead of being promised to the customer as exact.

## Step 9: What drives the predictions?

### Lasso coefficients

The lasso shrinks the coefficients of unhelpful predictors to exactly zero, so the features that survive are the ones the model finds useful. Predictors are standardized, so each coefficient is the change in predicted delivery days for a one-standard-deviation increase in that predictor (for a dummy variable, a one-standard-deviation change in the 0/1 indicator). Coefficients show direction and relative size, not causal effects.

```{r}
#| label: lasso-coefs
#| fig-cap: "Largest lasso coefficients (Recipe 3, standardized predictors)"
#| fig-height: 5.5
# Coefficients are per one standard deviation of each predictor; zero means the lasso dropped it
lasso_coefs <- tidy(fit_lasso3) |> filter(term != "(Intercept)")
n_kept  <- sum(lasso_coefs$estimate != 0)
n_total <- nrow(lasso_coefs)

top_coefs <- lasso_coefs |>
  filter(estimate != 0) |>
  slice_max(abs(estimate), n = 15) |>
  mutate(direction = if_else(estimate > 0, "Slower delivery", "Faster delivery"))

ggplot(top_coefs, aes(x = estimate, y = reorder(term, estimate), fill = direction)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Slower delivery" = "#d95f02", "Faster delivery" = "#1b9e77")) +
  labs(
    title = "Lasso: largest coefficients",
    x = "Change in predicted delivery days per 1 SD of the predictor",
    y = NULL, fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The lasso kept `r n_kept` of `r n_total` encoded predictors.

### Decision tree importance, grouped by original feature

A tree's raw importance scores are split across dummy columns, so a feature like `customer_state` appears as 27 small bars. We add the scores back together by original feature to get a clearer picture.

```{r}
#| label: tree-importance
#| fig-cap: "Decision tree importance, summed across dummy columns (Recipe 3)"
#| fig-height: 5
imp <- extract_fit_engine(fit_tree3)$variable.importance

imp_tbl <- tibble(term = names(imp), importance = imp) |>
  # A feature such as customer_state is split into many dummy columns; add them back together
  mutate(feature = case_when(
    str_detect(term, "^customer_state") ~ "customer_state",
    str_detect(term, "^seller_state")   ~ "seller_state",
    str_detect(term, "^same_state")     ~ "same_state",
    str_detect(term, "^same_region")    ~ "same_region",
    str_detect(term, "^cust_region")    ~ "customer_zip_region",
    str_detect(term, "^seller_region")  ~ "seller_zip_region",
    str_detect(term, "^purchase_year")  ~ "purchase_year",
    str_detect(term, "^purchase_month") ~ "purchase_month",
    str_detect(term, "^purchase_dow")   ~ "purchase_weekday",
    str_detect(term, "^category")       ~ "product_category",
    TRUE ~ term
  )) |>
  group_by(feature) |>
  summarise(importance = sum(importance), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(share = importance / sum(importance)) |>
  arrange(desc(importance))

imp_tbl |>
  slice_head(n = 12) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = share, y = reorder(feature, share))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2b8cbe") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(
    title = "Decision tree: share of importance by feature (Recipe 3)",
    x = "Share of total importance", y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
#| label: importance-values
#| include: false
top3 <- imp_tbl |> slice_head(n = 3)
timing_share <- imp_tbl |>
  filter(feature %in% c("purchase_month", "purchase_year", "purchase_weekday")) |>
  summarise(s = sum(share)) |> pull(s)
```

### Key takeaways on drivers

- **Route features dominate.** The three most important feature groups in the tree are `r top3$feature[1]` (`r scales::percent(top3$share[1], accuracy = 1)`), `r top3$feature[2]` (`r scales::percent(top3$share[2], accuracy = 1)`), and `r top3$feature[3]` (`r scales::percent(top3$share[3], accuracy = 1)`). Where an item travels from and to is the strongest driver of delivery time.
- **Purchase timing contributes a smaller share** (`r scales::percent(timing_share, accuracy = 1)` for year, month, and weekday combined), consistent with the exploration page's finding that purchase timing barely changes delivery outcomes. The months that do show up match the slow months seen in the exploration.
- **`estimated_days` ranks high in importance but added little to accuracy.** The tree uses it often, but because route features carry much of the same information, removing it costs little. Importance measures how much a feature is *used*; the recipe comparison measures how much accuracy it *adds*.
- **Caution:** correlated features share credit in tree importance, and neither the lasso nor the tree shows causation. These results describe what the models rely on to predict, not what causes a delay.

```{r}
write_rds(fit_lasso3, "data/final_lasso_r3.rds")
```

# Key Takeaways and Limitations

**What we found**

- Delivery time on Olist is driven mainly by **route** (seller and customer location), with product and order characteristics adding a smaller amount and purchase timing adding little.
- The best model (`r best_row$model`, `r best_row$recipe`) predicts delivery time to within about `r round(best_row$mae, 1)` days on average and explains about `r round(100 * best_row$rsq_trad)`% of the variation, improving MAE by `r round(100 * (1 - best_row$mae / draft_mae))`% over the first draft and `r round(100 * (1 - best_row$mae / naive_mae))`% over the naive average.
- Model choice mattered far less than feature choice: ridge, lasso, and linear regression perform almost identically, and the decision tree is only slightly different.
- Olist's own estimate carries limited extra information once route features are present, which supports the earlier finding that the estimates are conservative rather than precise.

**How far to trust it**

- **Single random split.** All results come from one test set. Differences of a few hundredths of a day between models are not meaningful, and a different random split would shift the numbers slightly.
- **Similar orders, not future orders.** The split is random across 2016-2018, so it tests performance on orders like those already seen. It does not test how the model would perform after a carrier change, a strike, or a seasonal shift.
- **Tail delays are still hard.** The model tends to under-predict the slowest orders, so a point estimate should be paired with a delivery window.
- **Order-item grain.** `delivery_days` is an order-level duration repeated across the items of an order, so multi-item orders carry slightly more weight in the metrics.
- **Settings chosen on one validation slice.** Tuning used a single validation set. If a chosen setting sits at the edge of its search grid (see the Settings column), a wider search might change results slightly.
- **Interpretation of coefficients.** Standardized lasso coefficients show direction and relative size, not causal effects.
- **Unmeasured factors.** Carrier performance, weather, seller behavior, and true seller-to-customer distance are not in the data. Zip-code region is only a coarse stand-in for distance.

**What could improve it**

Adding real seller-to-customer distance (from Olist's geolocation table) is the most promising next step. Non-linear ensemble models or a log-transformed target are further options that were outside the scope of this analysis.
